findings.title: Building a certificate authority for the whole Internet
findings.summary_md: Cloudflare's own announcement, published the day before press pickup, states its intent to become a public certificate authority. It has applied to the Chrome, Apple, Microsoft and Mozilla root programs, signed a definitive agreement to acquire a GlobalSign root trusted since 2012, and plans first production Merkle Tree Certificates in Q1 2027. Issuance will be ACME-first and conditional on client support for ACME Renewal Information (RFC 9773), with reproducible builds, attested hardware security modules and a public issuance dashboard planned.

findings.title: Building a post-quantum certificate authority with Merkle Tree Certificates
findings.summary_md: Companion post by Mari Galicer detailing the post-quantum CA architecture: free standard MTC issuance targeting Chrome's Quantum-resistant Root Store in early 2027, an ACME stack forked from Let's Encrypt's Boulder, and a mirroring cosigner built on the open-source Azul log, with Chrome's draft policy requiring at least two cosignatures per issuance log. It reports that the Chrome Beta 146 experiment served billions of MTCs with median handshakes 9 percent faster than classical chains before winding down in August 2026.

findings.title: Cultivating a robust and efficient quantum-safe HTTPS
findings.summary_md: Chrome's announcement of the Quantum-resistant Root Store program seven months before the Cloudflare story. Phase 1 is the feasibility study with Cloudflare already underway, Phase 2 in Q1 2027 bootstraps public MTCs with established CT log operators, and Phase 3 in Q3 2027 finalizes CA onboarding requirements for the Chrome Quantum-resistant Root Store. Chrome states it has no immediate plan to add traditional X.509 certificates carrying post-quantum signatures to its existing root store and expects ACME-only workflows.

findings.title: A Post-Quantum Future for Let's Encrypt
findings.summary_md: Let's Encrypt committed to Merkle Tree Certificates as its post-quantum path, targeting a staging MTC environment in late 2026 and production in 2027. The post quantifies the size problem: an ML-DSA-44 signature is roughly 2,420 bytes against 64 bytes for ECDSA P-256, a typical handshake carries five signatures and two public keys, and naive substitution would push handshakes past 10 kilobytes, citing Cloudflare research that a meaningful share of TLS connections then fail on real networks. It also cites NIST draft guidance that would disallow RSA-2048 and P-256 after 2035.
